Georges Danton. Born in 1759, this charismatic revolutionary leader rose to prominence during the early radical phase of the French Revolution. He was a founding member of the Cordeliers Club, one of the revolution's most influential radical societies, and later became a rival power base to Robespierre's faction. In 1793, he served on the Committee of Public Safety, but quickly clashed with Robespierre over the scale of executions during the Terror. Danton argued that terror should have limits and that clemency should prevail, a position Robespierre branded as treason and weakness. Danton advocated for ending the Terror and negotiating peace with foreign enemies, but these calls for moderation sealed his fate. In late 1793, he attempted to flee France, but then made a fatal political miscalculation and returned voluntarily. He was arrested, and in March and April of 1794, he was tried alongside Camille Desmoulins, a journalist and his friend, on charges of plotting against the republic. They were both executed by guillotine on April 5, 1794. Danton reportedly mocked the tribunal and proclaimed that his final words should be carried along with his decapitated head to show the crowd. His death marked the radicals' purge of moderate voices and the peak of the Reign of Terror.
